extracted.intended_audience: literate London readers, essayists, playwrights, and theatre-goers (early 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and implicit standards for writing and judging plays, essays, and social satire — including what makes tragedy and comedy effective, how actors influence reception, and how a social critic should conduct themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy effectiveness: incidents over wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul is not to be moved by words, but things; for the incidents in this drama are laid together so happily, that the spectator makes the play for himself, by the force which the circumstance has upon his imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy's power comes from the arrangement and force of its incidents and circumstances rather than from fine or correct lines. Even with dry discourse or improper expressions, well-chosen incidents can move an unprejudiced audience to pity; the spectator supplies emotional content from circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy genius: discernment of spirit and unifying motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's great address in showing covetousness the motive of the actions of the Puritan, the epicure, the gamester, and the trader ... shows he had to a great perfection, that discernment of spirit, which constitutes a genius for comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A masterful comedy uncovers a single underlying motive (e.g., covetousness) that unites diverse characters. Demonstrating insight into human drives — 'discernment of spirit' — is a hallmark of comic genius. Use this unifying vice to explain differing behaviors across character types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene construction: dramatize resistance to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene in the fourth act, where all the cheated people oppose the man that would open their eyes, has something in it so inimitably excellent...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct scenes that dramatize collective self-deception and the resistance of people to being undeceived; such oppositional crowd scenes can be powerfully effective and memorable in both comedy and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting matters: actor's person and behaviour affect reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The person and behaviour of Mr. Wilks has no small share in conducing to the popularity of the play ... when a handsome fellow is going to a more coarse exit ... his shape and countenance make every tender one reprieve him with all her heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An actor's physical presence, countenance, and manner can significantly influence audience sympathy and the success of a play—sometimes redeeming weak text. Casting and performance choices are thus integral to dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct of social criticism: observe things, forbear persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The age you live in is such, that a good picture of any vice or virtue will infallibly be misrepresented ... all will resent the ill characters you produce, out of fear of their own turn in the licence you must be obliged to take, if you point at particular persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing satire or moral observation, avoid targeting identifiable individuals. Present general pictures of vice and virtue; be a reformer rather than an inquisitor. Generalized portraits reduce backlash and make the critique more durable and principled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by concrete detail and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of characters (e.g., Frank Careless and Will Nice) emphasize small habitual gestures and dress-adjusting habits to mark coxcomb versus fop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters through repeated small actions, habitual gestures, and dress, rather than abstract labels. Distinguishing behavior (studied negligence vs. laborious exactness) reveals social type effectively and economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraying gambling/addiction: alternating extremes and ruined scale
rubrics_metrics.description: There appeared no middle condition; the triumph of a prince, or the misery of a beggar, were his alternate states ... In the morning at twelve, we were worth four thousand pounds; at three, we were arrived at six thousand; ... to nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To depict a gamester convincingly, dramatize extreme, rapid swings of fortune and mood. Show obsession through numerical rises and falls and the reduction from great wealth to beggary to illuminate the destructive arc of gambling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and personified 'familiar' as observational device
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's familiar recounts three stations (a beauty, a common swearer, a gamester) to illustrate how spirits/observers notice human follies and inform conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a framing device or persona (e.g., a 'familiar' spirit) to gather and relay vignettes that exemplify types or morals. Such devices allow the author to collect representative incidents and deliver moral or social observations without direct personal attack.
